# Summary

**Question.** Can the pre-treatment CD8 T-cell compartment predict response to immune
checkpoint blockade (ICB)?

**Result.** Non-responders carry a significantly higher fraction of exhausted CD8
T cells at baseline (median **62.4%** vs **50.0%**; mean 60.6% vs 44.4%).

| Operationalization | Statistic | p | AUROC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Module-score ratio (memory-like − exhausted) | Wilcoxon W=11 | **0.0041** | 0.878 |
| CLR-composition, exhausted fraction | Wilcoxon W=79 | **0.0041** (Bonf. 0.017) | 0.878 |
| Raw exhausted fraction | Wilcoxon W=77 | **0.0076** | **0.856** |

Three independent parameterizations converge on **AUROC ≈ 0.85–0.88** (n = 19
baseline patients; 10 non-responders / 9 responders).

**Key refinement over the naive analysis.** The signal is **reduced exhaustion**,
not **expanded memory-like cells**. The memory-like compartment differs at the
*program* level (module score p = 0.022) but **not** in *absolute abundance*
(composition p = 0.50). Averaging a memory-like module across all CD8s is
mechanically lifted by a lower exhausted burden; the cluster-composition test
dissociates the two and shows exhaustion carries the signal.

**Two analytical decisions that changed the answer** (Sections 4 and 5):

1. Automated reference annotation (SingleR/Monaco) **under-called exhausted CD8s**,
   assigning ~2,900 of them to a generic `T cells` bucket. Gating on the SingleR
   label alone would have discarded the arm of the contrast doing the work.
2. A ~1,270-cell **γδ T-cell** cluster was mislabeled as NK + generic T. γδ cells
   share cytotoxic markers (NKG7/GNLY/KLRD1) with CD8s and would have contaminated
   the CD8 pool under a cytotoxicity-based gate.

---

# Data and design

**GSE120575** — Sade-Feldman et al., *Cell* 2018. CD45+ tumor-infiltrating immune
cells from melanoma biopsies taken before or after anti-CTLA4 / anti-PD1 /
combination therapy. **Smart-seq2** (plate-based, full-length, one cell per well).

- **55,737 genes × 16,291 cells** after load.
- **Baseline (Pre): 19 patients — 10 non-responders, 9 responders.**
- Post-treatment: 29 samples (21 NR / 8 R) — **not used** (see Limitations).

**Design decisions, fixed a priori:**

| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Endpoint | Provided Responder / Non-responder | Deposit-level label. Durable clinical benefit (PFS/OS) would be preferable. |
| Timepoint | **Baseline (Pre) only** | A *predictive* biomarker must exist before dosing. On-treatment data informs mechanism, not enrollment. |
| Unit of analysis | **Patient (n=19)**, never cell | Cells within a patient are pseudoreplicates. |
| Intended use | Trial enrichment | Endgame is a small, locked, deployable signature. |

**Tissue caveat.** These are tumor-infiltrating cells, not PBMC. A deployable
enrichment biomarker would need to be blood-based; tumor is used here because the
response signal is strong and the labels are clean.

---

# Load

Two GEO quirks required handling.

**(1) The TPM matrix has a two-row header with a one-column offset.** Row 1 = cell
names (first field blank), row 2 = `Pre_P#`/`Post_P#` sample labels, row 3+ = gene
symbol in column 1 then TPM values. The file has 16,292 columns = 1 gene column +
16,291 cells.

**(2) `data.table::fread` fails** on this file — 16,291 columns overflows R's
`2^31-1` byte character-string limit during parsing. `readr` streams incrementally
and works, but its default 128 KB connection buffer is smaller than a single line.

```{r load-expr}
Sys.setenv(VROOM_CONNECTION_SIZE = 500000)   # MUST precede any readr call

library(readr); library(Matrix); library(Seurat); library(dplyr); library(tidyr)

f_tpm  <- "GSE120575_Sade_Feldman_melanoma_single_cells_TPM_GEO.txt.gz"
f_meta <- "GSE120575_patient_ID_single_cells.txt.gz"

## Row 1 = cell names, offset by one blank leading field
hdr <- read_lines(f_tpm, n_max = 2)
cell_names <- strsplit(hdr[1], "\t")[[1]]
cell_names <- cell_names[cell_names != "" & !is.na(cell_names)]
stopifnot(length(cell_names) == 16291)

## Rows 3+ : gene symbol in col 1, TPM thereafter
dat   <- read_tsv(f_tpm, skip = 2, col_names = FALSE, show_col_types = FALSE)
genes <- dat[[1]]
expr  <- as.matrix(dat[, -1]); mode(expr) <- "numeric"
if (ncol(expr) == length(cell_names) + 1) expr <- expr[, -ncol(expr)]  # trailing NA col

rownames(expr) <- make.unique(as.character(genes))
colnames(expr) <- cell_names
expr <- Matrix(expr, sparse = TRUE)
cat("expr:", nrow(expr), "genes x", ncol(expr), "cells\n")   # 55737 x 16291
```

**(3) The metadata file is a GEO submission template.** A 19-line preamble precedes
the real table (header on line 20). The submitter misspelled "patient" as
**`patinet`** in the column name — matching only the correct spelling silently
returns `NA`. There are also 24 blank rows and a stray `type` row.

```{r load-meta}
library(data.table)
meta_raw <- fread(f_meta, skip = "Sample name", header = TRUE, sep = "\t",
                  data.table = FALSE, fill = TRUE)

col_title    <- grep("^title$",         colnames(meta_raw), value = TRUE)[1]
col_patient  <- grep("patient|patinet", colnames(meta_raw), ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)[1]
col_response <- grep("response",        colnames(meta_raw), ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)[1]
col_therapy  <- grep("therapy",         colnames(meta_raw), ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)[1]

meta <- data.frame(
  cell     = meta_raw[[col_title]],
  pt_field = meta_raw[[col_patient]],     # "Pre_P1" / "Post_P28_2"
  response = meta_raw[[col_response]],    # "Responder" / "Non-responder" (exact strings)
  therapy  = meta_raw[[col_therapy]],
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

## Strip template junk: 24 blank rows + stray 'type' row
meta <- meta[!is.na(meta$cell) & meta$cell != "" & meta$cell != "type", ]
meta <- meta[!duplicated(meta$cell), ]
meta$timepoint <- ifelse(grepl("^Pre",  meta$pt_field), "Pre",
                  ifelse(grepl("^Post", meta$pt_field), "Post", NA))
meta$patient   <- sub("^(Pre|Post)_", "", meta$pt_field)
meta <- meta[meta$response %in% c("Responder","Non-responder") &
             meta$timepoint %in% c("Pre","Post"), ]
rownames(meta) <- meta$cell
stopifnot(nrow(meta) == 16291)           # exact match to the expression matrix
```

```{r build-obj}
common <- intersect(colnames(expr), rownames(meta))
expr <- expr[, common]; meta <- meta[common, ]

obj <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = expr, meta.data = meta, project = "GSE120575")
## NOTE: the 'counts' slot holds TPM, not raw integer counts.
##       => differential expression uses limma on log-TPM, NOT DESeq2/edgeR.

pt_tab <- unique(obj@meta.data[, c("patient","timepoint","response")])
print(table(pt_tab$timepoint, pt_tab$response))
#         Non-responder Responder
#   Post             21         8
#   Pre              10         9
```

---

# QC, normalization, integration

**Platform-matched QC.** Smart-seq2 sorts one cell per well, so there is **no
ambient-RNA "soup"** and doublets are rare. `SoupX`/`CellBender` and aggressive
doublet calling are droplet (10x) tools and are deliberately **not** run here.

Observed distributions confirm high-quality, FACS-sorted input:

- `nFeature_RNA`: bulk 1,500–5,000 (tail to ~9,000) — the deep coverage expected
  of full-length plate-based protocols.
- `percent.mt`: **maximum ~4%** — dying cells were largely excluded at the bench.
  The `< 20` cutoff is far more lenient than the data requires and removes nothing;
  it is retained for convention.

```{r qc}
obj[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(obj, pattern = "^MT-")
VlnPlot(obj, c("nFeature_RNA","nCount_RNA","percent.mt"), pt.size = 0)

## Confound check BEFORE trusting anything: is batch collinear with response?
print(table(obj$patient, obj$response))

obj <- subset(obj, subset = nFeature_RNA > 500 & nFeature_RNA < 9000 & percent.mt < 20)

obj <- NormalizeData(obj) |>
       FindVariableFeatures(nfeatures = 2000) |>
       ScaleData() |>
       RunPCA(npcs = 30)

library(harmony)
obj <- RunHarmony(obj, group.by.vars = "patient")
obj <- RunUMAP(obj, reduction = "harmony", dims = 1:30)
obj <- FindNeighbors(obj, reduction = "harmony", dims = 1:30)
obj <- FindClusters(obj, resolution = 0.6)

DimPlot(obj, group.by = "response")
```

### Reading the response UMAP

Responders and non-responders are **thoroughly intermixed across every cluster**.
This is the expected and desired result, not a null finding:

- Response is **not** a global transcriptomic shift. Clean separation of R vs NR on
  a UMAP would be *suspicious* — typically a batch confound driving the split.
- The intermixing confirms **Harmony integrated correctly**: groups are not
  separated by patient/batch artifact.
- The signal lives in **proportions and states of specific subsets**, which a
  whole-population embedding cannot display. This is precisely why the analysis
  must be differential-abundance and cell-state-resolved rather than bulk.

---

# Annotation: where automated labels fail

```{r singler}
library(SingleR); library(celldex)
ref  <- celldex::MonacoImmuneData()
sce  <- as.SingleCellExperiment(obj)
pred <- SingleR(test = sce, ref = ref, labels = ref$label.main)
obj$SingleR.main <- pred$labels
print(table(obj$SingleR.main))
```

```
        B cells       Basophils    CD4+ T cells    CD8+ T cells Dendritic cells
           1777               6            3241            4022             588
      Monocytes     Neutrophils        NK cells     Progenitors         T cells
           1154               8             546               3            4945
```

## Problem 1 — 4,945 cells in a generic `T cells` bucket

Cross-tabulating SingleR labels against Harmony clusters shows the ambiguous bucket
is **concentrated exactly where CD8s live**:

| Cluster | CD8+ T | generic `T cells` | CD4+ T |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1,667 | **1,504** | 20 |
| 2 | 564 | **730** | 14 |
| 6 | 429 | **453** | 9 |

In each, the generic bucket roughly *equals* the confident CD8 calls, with CD4
essentially absent. These are CD8s that **downregulated canonical markers — the
exhaustion signature itself**. Gating on `SingleR.main == "CD8+ T cells"` would
have discarded ~2,900 CD8s, disproportionately the exhausted ones, biasing the
analysis against the very contrast being tested.

## Problem 2 — a γδ T-cell cluster mislabeled as NK

```{r markers}
mk <- c("CD3D","CD3E","CD2", "CD8A","CD8B", "CD4","IL7R","FOXP3","CTLA4",
        "NCAM1","KLRD1","NKG7","GNLY","FCGR3A", "TRDC","TRGC1",
        "TCF7","SELL","LEF1", "HAVCR2","LAG3","PDCD1","TOX","ENTPD1")
avg <- AverageExpression(obj, features = mk, group.by = "seurat_clusters",
                         assays = "RNA", layer = "data")$RNA
print(round(as.matrix(avg), 2))
DotPlot(obj, features = mk, group.by = "seurat_clusters") + RotatedAxis()
```

**Cluster 4** (~1,270 cells): `TRDC` **6.77**, `TRGC1` 2.77, `CD3D` 4.15, `CD3E` 3.47
— but `CD8A` 0.64, `CD8B` 0.15, `CD4` 0.08. Unambiguously T lineage, negative for
both co-receptors, with a dominant **γδ TCR constant-chain signal**.

SingleR split these across "NK cells" (302) and generic "T cells" (948) because
`label.main` has no γδ category. Genuine NK would be **CD3D-negative** (here 4.15);
`NCAM1` is only 0.52. There is **no clean NK cluster in this dataset** — the "NK"
calls were largely misassigned γδ T cells. Because γδ cells share NKG7/GNLY/KLRD1
with CD8s, a cytotoxicity-based gate would have swept them into the CD8 pool.

**Cluster 3** shows `CD4` 2.78 but `CD3D` 0.31 and `FCGR3A` 2.85 — **monocytes
express CD4**. Gating CD4 T cells on CD4 alone would import the myeloid
compartment. Hence: **pan-T gate (`CD3D`/`CD3E`) first, co-receptor second.**

## Marker-validated lineage assignment

```{r gate}
## CD3D+ / CD8A+ / CD8B+ / CD4-low
cd8_core <- c("1","2","6","8")
cd8 <- subset(obj, subset = seurat_clusters %in% cd8_core)

## Recover genuine CD8s from mixed clusters (7,9,11: CD8A 3.4-4.0 but CD4 1.5-1.7,
## FOXP3 present) by per-cell gating rather than majority vote
mixed <- subset(obj, subset = seurat_clusters %in% c("7","9","11"))
cd8_cells_mixed <- WhichCells(mixed, expression = CD8A > 1 & CD4 < 0.5 & CD3D > 1)
cd8 <- merge(cd8, subset(mixed, cells = cd8_cells_mixed))

## Document γδ explicitly rather than silently dropping them
obj$lineage <- dplyr::case_when(
  obj$seurat_clusters == "4"                              ~ "gdT",
  obj$seurat_clusters %in% cd8_core                       ~ "CD8T",
  obj$seurat_clusters %in% c("0","10")                    ~ "CD4T",
  obj$seurat_clusters %in% c("3","12")                    ~ "Myeloid",
  obj$seurat_clusters %in% c("5","13","14","15","16","17")~ "B",
  TRUE                                                    ~ "Mixed_T"
)
print(table(obj$lineage))
#       B    CD4T    CD8T     gdT Mixed_T Myeloid
#    1875    3577    6297    1272    1491    1778
cat("CD8 cells gated:", ncol(cd8), "\n")   # 6936  (vs SingleR's 4022)
```

## CD8 state definitions

The memory/exhaustion axis is directly readable from the marker table:

| Cluster | TCF7 | IL7R | PDCD1 | HAVCR2 | TOX | LAG3 | Assignment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **2** | 1.63 | 2.77 | 1.34 | 1.13 | 1.04 | 1.49 | **memory-like** |
| **1** | 0.84 | 1.06 | **3.15** | **2.96** | **1.99** | 1.94 | **exhausted** |
| **6** | 1.03 | 1.48 | **2.55** | 2.39 | 1.76 | 1.88 | **exhausted** |
| 8 | — | — | — | — | — | — | intermediate |

# Baseline subset and the metadata inconsistency

Two patients (**P4**, **P28**) carry **opposite response labels at Pre vs Post
under identical therapy** (`anti-CTLA4+PD1`):

| patient | sample | timepoint | therapy | response |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P28 | Post_P28 | Post | anti-CTLA4+PD1 | Non-responder |
| P28 | Pre_P28 | Pre | anti-CTLA4+PD1 | **Responder** |
| P4 | Post_P4 | Post | anti-CTLA4+PD1 | Responder |
| P4 | Pre_P4 | Pre | anti-CTLA4+PD1 | **Non-responder** |

Response cannot flip for one patient on one therapy course. The most likely reading
is that **patient IDs are not reliably stable across timepoints in this deposit**,
or that lesion-level labels were attached inconsistently at submission (P28 also has
both `Post_P28` and `Post_P28_2`; multi-lesion sampling is in play). This is not
resolvable from the metadata alone and is reported as an unresolved caveat.

**Consequence — and why the a priori baseline-only design protects us:** every `_2`
suffixed sample is **Post**; there are no `_2` samples in the Pre set. All 19
baseline samples carry exactly one response label. The inconsistency threatens only
*paired* Pre→Post analyses, which are therefore **not attempted**.

```{r baseline}
cd8_base <- subset(cd8, subset = timepoint == "Pre")
cd8_base$patient <- sub("^Pre_", "", cd8_base$pt_field)
cd8_base <- JoinLayers(cd8_base)   # merge() left split layers; MUST rejoin before aggregating

chk <- unique(cd8_base@meta.data[, c("patient","response")])
stopifnot(!any(duplicated(chk$patient)))   # hard guard: one label per patient
print(table(chk$response))                 # 10 Non-responder / 9 Responder
cat("baseline CD8 cells:", ncol(cd8_base), "\n")   # 2651
print(table(cd8_base$patient, cd8_base$response))
```

**Minimum-cell threshold.** Per-patient CD8 yield ranges **33–257**. A ≥20-cell
floor is declared a priori; every patient clears it, so it removes nothing. The
thinnest patients (P6 = 33, P26 = 34, P35 = 55) are addressed by sensitivity
analysis below rather than by exclusion.

---

# Result 1 — Module scores

```{r modules}
memory_like <- list(c("TCF7","IL7R","CCR7","SELL","LEF1","GZMK"))
exhausted   <- list(c("HAVCR2","LAG3","PDCD1","TIGIT","CTLA4","ENTPD1","TOX"))

cd8_base <- NormalizeData(cd8_base)
cd8_base <- AddModuleScore(cd8_base, features = memory_like, name = "MemoryLike")
cd8_base <- AddModuleScore(cd8_base, features = exhausted,   name = "Exhausted")

## Collapse to the patient — the unit of analysis
pt_scores <- cd8_base@meta.data |>
  group_by(patient, response) |>
  summarise(n_cd8 = n(),
            mem   = mean(MemoryLike1),
            exh   = mean(Exhausted1),
            ratio = mem - exh,          # module scores are already centered
            .groups = "drop")

wilcox.test(mem   ~ response, data = pt_scores)   # W=17, p=0.022
wilcox.test(exh   ~ response, data = pt_scores)   # W=71, p=0.035
wilcox.test(ratio ~ response, data = pt_scores)   # W=11, p=0.0041  <- primary
```

| Score | W | p | Direction | NR mean | R mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory-like | 17 | 0.022 | R higher | −0.099 | +0.156 |
| Exhaustion | 71 | 0.035 | **NR higher** | −0.024 | −0.293 |
| **Balance (mem − exh)** | **11** | **0.0041** | R higher | −0.075 | **+0.449** |

The **balance is stronger than either component**, consistent with the original
claim that it is the *ratio* of states, not either alone, that tracks response.
`ratio` is the **pre-specified primary endpoint** — the three tests are not
independent (`ratio` is derived from the other two), and it survives Bonferroni
(0.0041 × 3 = 0.012).

`W = 11` of 90 possible pairs ⇒ responders exceed non-responders in 79/90 pairs ⇒
**univariate AUROC = 0.878**.

```{r modules-plot}
pt_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(pt_scores, c(mem, exh, ratio),
                               names_to = "score", values_to = "value")
ggplot2::ggplot(pt_long, ggplot2::aes(response, value, fill = response)) +
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = .6) +
  ggplot2::geom_jitter(width = .15, size = 2) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~score, scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::theme_bw() + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "per-patient mean module score")
```

---

# Result 2 — Composition (independent methodology)

Module scores depend on gene-list choice. Differential abundance of
marker-validated clusters is the more robust framing. Proportions are
**compositional** (a fixed pie — one fraction rising forces others down), so a
centered log-ratio transform is applied rather than naive proportion tests.

```{r composition}
cd8_base$cd8_state <- dplyr::case_when(
  cd8_base$seurat_clusters == "2"          ~ "memlike",
  cd8_base$seurat_clusters %in% c("1","6") ~ "exhausted",
  cd8_base$seurat_clusters == "8"          ~ "intermediate",
  TRUE                                     ~ "other"
)
print(table(cd8_base$cd8_state, cd8_base$response))

comp <- cd8_base@meta.data |>
  dplyr::count(patient, response, cd8_state) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = cd8_state, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

cnt <- as.matrix(comp[, setdiff(names(comp), c("patient","response"))])
clr <- function(x){ x <- x + 0.5; log(x) - rowMeans(log(x)) }
comp_clr <- as.data.frame(clr(cnt)); comp_clr$response <- comp$response

for (s in setdiff(colnames(comp_clr), "response"))
  print(wilcox.test(comp_clr[[s]] ~ comp_clr$response))
```

| CD8 state | NR cells | R cells | W | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **exhausted** | 1,063 | 447 | **79** | **0.0041** (Bonf. 4× = 0.017) |
| memlike | 358 | 289 | 36 | 0.50 |
| intermediate | 156 | 103 | 48 | 0.84 |
| other | 126 | 109 | 29 | 0.21 |

**⇒ 1,063/1,703 = 62% of NR CD8s are exhausted vs 447/948 = 47% of R CD8s.**

## The methods disagree — and the disagreement is the finding

Composition confirms **exhaustion** (p = 0.0041) but **not memory-like abundance**
(p = 0.50), whereas module scores showed both. They measure different things:

- **Composition** asks *how many cells fall in the memory-like cluster?*
- **Module score** asks *how strongly do CD8s express the program, averaged across all of them?*

Responders do not have **more** memory-like cells — they have CD8s that are **less
exhausted overall**. Because the module score averages across every CD8, a lower
exhausted burden mechanically lifts the mean memory-like score with no change in
memory-like cluster size. Discrete cluster assignment is also coarse (a cell just
over a boundary counts fully), while the continuous score captures gradations.

**Conclusion: the finding is about exhaustion burden.** Both methods agree there,
at identical p and near-identical W-magnitude.

## Raw fraction (most interpretable)

```{r fraction}
frac <- cd8_base@meta.data |>
  dplyr::count(patient, response, cd8_state) |>
  dplyr::group_by(patient, response) |>
  dplyr::mutate(frac = n/sum(n)) |>
  dplyr::filter(cd8_state == "exhausted")

frac |> dplyr::group_by(response) |>
  dplyr::summarise(median_frac = median(frac), mean_frac = mean(frac))
wilcox.test(frac ~ response, data = frac)    # W=77, p=0.0076
pROC::roc(response ~ frac, data = frac)      # AUC = 0.8556
```

|  | median | mean |
|---|---|---|
| Non-responder | **0.624** | 0.606 |
| Responder | **0.500** | 0.444 |

`pROC` independently confirms direction (*controls > cases*). **AUROC = 0.856.**
A ~16-point absolute difference in exhausted burden — a clinically legible effect,
not a statistical curiosity.

### Per-patient structure (honest overlap)

- Cleanest responders: **P8 (14.8%)**, **P26 (23.5%)**
- Cleanest non-responders: **P2 (73.4%)**, **P27 (70.0%)**, **P12 (67.5%)**
- Overlap zone ~50–57%: P1 (55.2%), P28 (55.7%), P29 (57.1%) are responders in
  non-responder territory; **P3 (35.3%)** is a non-responder with responder-like
  low exhaustion.

At a 55% cutoff, **~4 of 19 patients misclassify**. This is a population-level
shift with real predictive value, **not a clean separator** — which is exactly why
no locked blood biomarker exists for ICB response.

---

# Robustness

```{r robustness}
## 1. Cell-depth sensitivity — does the result survive dropping thin patients?
pt_thick <- dplyr::filter(pt_scores, n_cd8 >= 50)      # 17 of 19 retained
wilcox.test(ratio ~ response, data = pt_thick)          # W=10, p=0.011

## 2. Is the signal an artifact of sequencing depth?
cor.test(pt_scores$n_cd8, pt_scores$ratio, method = "spearman")
# rho = -0.349, p = 0.143

## 3. Therapy confound
ther <- cd8_base@meta.data |> dplyr::distinct(patient, response, therapy)
print(table(ther$therapy, ther$response))
fisher.test(table(ther$therapy, ther$response))        # p = 0.271

## 4. Largest homogeneous stratum: anti-PD1 only
pd1 <- pt_scores |> dplyr::left_join(ther, by = c("patient","response")) |>
  dplyr::filter(therapy == "anti-PD1")
wilcox.test(ratio ~ response, data = pd1)              # W=7, p=0.15, n=12 (8 NR / 4 R)
```

**Depth sensitivity — passed.** Excluding P6 and P26 (n=17) preserves the effect
(p = 0.011); the rise from 0.0041 is the power cost of two fewer patients. The
result does not depend on P26's extreme value on 34 cells.

**Depth confound — passed, conservatively.** rho = −0.35, p = 0.14. The *negative*
sign means higher-yield patients trend toward *more* exhaustion; depth works
slightly **against** a spurious responder signal.

**Therapy — descriptively imbalanced, not statistically demonstrable.**

| | NR | R |
|---|---|---|
| anti-CTLA4 | 1 | 1 |
| anti-CTLA4+PD1 | 1 | 4 |
| anti-PD1 | **8** | 4 |

Fisher **p = 0.27** — therapy–response association can be neither demonstrated nor
excluded at n = 19. Within the anti-PD1 stratum the effect is **directionally
preserved**: W = 7 of 32 (null expectation 16), 25/32 pairs (78%) in the expected
direction, **AUROC 0.78**, p = 0.15 at n = 12. The exact test *could* have reached
significance here (minimum achievable p ≈ 0.004), so this is genuine underpowering
rather than a floor effect.

---

# Why no multivariate classifier

A single mechanistically-motivated feature already yields **AUROC 0.88**. At n = 19,
a lasso over dozens of features will either re-select the same signal or overfit to
a spurious improvement. **The ratio is the signature.** One interpretable biological
feature at AUROC 0.88 is a stronger and more defensible claim than a multi-feature
model at this sample size.

Had a classifier been fit, the non-negotiable guards would be: split **by patient**
(here automatic — each row *is* a patient), feature selection **inside** the CV loop,
and leave-one-patient-out CV.

---

# Limitations

1. **External validation not performed.** Signatures that shine in discovery and
   evaporate on an independent cohort are the norm. This is the required next step
   (GSE115978, or a bulk melanoma ICB cohort scored via a rank-based signature).
2. **Predictive vs prognostic not established.** Without an untreated control arm,
   it cannot be shown that exhaustion burden predicts benefit *from this drug*
   rather than general disease severity. The drug-mechanism coherence (checkpoint
   blockade acts on the exhaustion axis) is supporting, not dispositive.
3. **Therapy imbalance** (above) — neither demonstrated nor excluded.
4. **Tumor, not blood.** Not deployable for enrollment; a PBMC-based equivalent is
   the translational path.
5. **n = 19.** Adequate for patient-level nonparametric testing; not for locking a
   clinical cutoff.
6. **Metadata inconsistency** (P4/P28) — paired Pre→Post analyses not attempted.
7. **Endpoint** is the deposit's R/NR label, not durable clinical benefit (PFS/OS).
8. **Exhaustion module contains `CTLA4`/`TIGIT`**, which are broad; the axis holds
   on PDCD1/HAVCR2/LAG3/TOX/ENTPD1 and is corroborated by cluster composition,
   which is gene-list-independent.

---

# Mechanistic interpretation

> **Responders carry a baseline CD8 compartment with a lower exhaustion burden —
> a larger reinvigoration-competent reserve for checkpoint blockade to mobilize.
> Non-responders arrive with CD8s already skewed toward a terminally exhausted
> state that checkpoint blockade cannot rescue.**

This is a *mechanism*, not a statistic, and that matters three ways. It is
falsifiable and biologically coherent, so it is defensible to partners and
regulators in a way that "our model has AUC 0.86" is not. It argues the marker is
**predictive** (linked to the drug's mode of action) rather than merely prognostic.
And read backwards, it converts a stratification biomarker into **target
discovery**: whatever enforces the terminally exhausted state in non-responders
becomes a candidate target for combination therapy — the drug-development funnel
running in reverse.
